title: Hurricane Lala Leaves One Dead, 100,000 Without Power Across Hawaii
excerpt: The Category 1 hurricane brought over three feet of rain to the Big Island, destroying bridges, sweeping homes off foundations and triggering a statewide recovery effort.
body:
• Hurricane Lala killed at least one person — a 90-year-old woman found dead in floodwaters on the Big Island — and damaged or destroyed over 100 homes across Hawaii.
  • The storm dumped more than three and a half feet of rain on the Big Island's mountains, triggering landslides that destroyed six bridges and collapsed a highway, trapping up to 2,500 residents.
  • Over 250,000 customers lost power at the storm's peak, with Hawaiian Electric warning that outages in rural areas could last weeks or months.
  • A marine heat wave and developing Super El Niño kept the storm unusually strong as it approached, defying the cooler ocean temperatures that typically weaken Pacific storms near Hawaii.

At least one person is dead and over 100,000 homes and businesses remain without power after Hurricane Lala swept south of the Hawaiian island chain over the weekend, unleashing torrential rainfall that triggered catastrophic flooding and landslides across multiple islands.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green confirmed Monday that a 90-year-old woman "perished in the flood" after being reported missing in a neighborhood in the south of the Big Island. Rescue crews from multiple agencies, including the National Guard, were dispatched to locate her.

Unprecedented Rainfall and Destruction

Lala strengthened to a Category 1 hurricane on Saturday, making its closest approach to the Big Island at around 5 p.m. local time with its eyewall brushing the southern coastline from roughly 30 miles away, according to the National Hurricane Center.

https://x.com/AP/status/2089276978998169899

The storm dumped over three and a half feet of rain on the Big Island's mountains and up to two feet on Maui's mountainous areas. Winds of up to 140 mph were measured atop Mauna Kea, the dormant volcano standing nearly 14,000 feet in elevation.

"It's the flood and the mud and the rock that poured through communities in the Big Island's south area that caused the real damage."

— Gov. Josh Green

In the Ka'u district of the Big Island, floodwater pushed at least two homes off their foundations. One was carried several hundred yards away, while a woman trying to reach her vehicle was swept up and hospitalized with moderate injuries. Six bridges were destroyed or nearly destroyed, and parts of Pahala Highway collapsed overnight, cutting off critical access to the area's only hospital and trapping up to 2,500 residents.

Power Outages Could Last Months

At its peak, the storm knocked out electricity to more than 250,000 customers across the island chain. By Monday afternoon, roughly 100,000 remained without power, according to PowerOutage.com. Hawaiian Electric warned that outages in the hardest-hit rural areas of the Big Island could last "weeks or even months," with major transmission lines crossing remote and mountainous terrain.

Some 500 utility workers, including crews flying in from the mainland United States, were deployed for restoration efforts. An additional 100 crew members from the mainland were expected by Tuesday.

Statewide Impact

On Oahu, the state's most populous island, the Honolulu Fire Department responded to 629 emergency calls, including 147 downed trees, 66 blown roofs, and 29 downed power lines. Ocean rescue crews conducted about 160 rescues between Friday and Saturday evening. Hawaii's state and county offices, schools, courts and judiciary offices were closed Monday, with Big Island facilities remaining closed through at least Tuesday.

Two airports on the Big Island — Hilo International and Ellison Onizuka Kona International — were temporarily closed Saturday. Hawaiian Airlines canceled 52 flights statewide Sunday, following 190 cancellations and delays the previous day. A statewide brown water advisory warned of contaminated stormwater in coastal waters and streams.

Climate Factors Fueled the Storm

Tropical storms approaching Hawaii typically weaken as they hit cooler ocean temperatures near the islands, according to CNN. Lala defied that pattern, maintaining its strength due to an ongoing marine heat wave extending to California and a developing Super El Niño that kept waters unusually warm.

No hurricane had previously made landfall on the Big Island in recorded history. The last hurricane to hit any part of Hawaii was 34 years ago.

Recovery Ahead

Federal and state officials have begun damage assessments as the storm, now a tropical storm, moves west over the open Pacific. Gov. Green said impacts could have been "much worse" had Lala tracked slightly farther north toward Oahu. Emergency officials urged residents to exercise caution during cleanup, warning that many casualties after natural disasters occur during recovery operations involving downed power lines, heavy equipment and generators.
nri_angle: Hawaii's diverse communities, including its significant South Asian and Indian-American populations, face weeks of recovery from the worst hurricane to hit the state in decades.
